On monomials the diagonal multipliers give the stated product trace norm and contractivity; strong continuity follows by density, and the positive damping margin on compact subsectors gives locally uniform operator-norm convergence of finite diagonal truncations. With decay U and phase V, |V|≤ρU. If the distance exceeds one, increasing the radius from e^{−U} to e^{−|V|/ρ} increases the squared distance at fixed phase; a coordinate maximizing the ratio supplies the approximating lattice and hence the reverse bound as t↓0. The squared-profile derivative has sign h with h′=(1+ρ²)e^u cos(ρu), giving exactly one interior maximum before the half-turn; the tail bound rules out every later lobe. The root equation is only used on the stated first-lobe interval. For small ρ, the phase differs from π/2+arctan ρ by O(exp(−π/(2ρ))), giving the prefactor ρ/e. For large ρ, the root forces sin(ρu)=O(1/ρ) on the second quadrant, then π−ρu=2/ρ+O(ρ⁻²), yielding the asserted large-angle law. The strict maximum gives a fixed gap outside a neighborhood, and monotonicity on either side reduces the local grid comparison to floor and ceiling. Taylor expansion with curvature −Dρ gives a uniform O(t³) even at a nearest-grid tie. The specified real times realize every phase distance in [0,1/2]. The nonrotating case gives norm one for every positive time. Inspected check.py without executing it.

value.rationale: The result identifies exactly how a compact analytic semigroup can be discontinuous in operator norm at time zero. The maximal rotation-to-damping ratio alone determines the jump in every finite diagonal dimension, and the exponentially small rise above one distinguishes weak rotation quantitatively. The scalar lattice law proves a sharp leading error with no single limiting second-order coefficient, an informative boundary that is missed by a plain O(t²) estimate.
